title: Race Underway to Choose the UN's Next Secretary-General
summary:
The race to become the next United Nations secretary-general is well underway. The winner will become the UN's 10th secretary-general, taking office on January 1, 2027, and succeeding António Guterres. This year's selection could be especially significant because the UN may choose its first-ever woman leader — seven candidates are running, four of whom are women. Based on the UN's informal regional rotation, a candidate from Latin America and the Caribbean is also considered likely.

The secretary-general is the UN's chief administrative officer and de facto head of the UN system. The role has been described as "equal parts diplomat and advocate, civil servant and CEO." It was created with the UN Charter in 1945, and the first appointment, Trygve Lie, took place in 1946. Richard Gowan of the International Crisis Group told the Council on Foreign Relations that the position is "remarkably powerless" yet "highly influential," because of the secretary-general's ability to use their public platform and shape global opinion.

The seven candidates are: Ivonne A-Baki, a former Ecuadorian ambassador; María Fernanda Espinosa Garcés, former president of the General Assembly; Rafael Mariano Grossi, director general of the International Atomic Energy Agency; Rebeca Grynspan Mayufis, a former vice president of Costa Rica; Olara Otunnu, a veteran Ugandan diplomat; Carolyn Rodrigues Birkett, Guyana's current UN ambassador; and Macky Sall, former president of Senegal.

The process is set out in Article 97 of the UN Charter, which says the secretary-general "shall be appointed by the General Assembly upon the recommendation of the Security Council." In practice, it is complicated and often takes more than a year. Candidates must be nominated by at least one member state, then submit a vision statement, CV, and campaign financing disclosures. They also participate in public town halls and interactive dialogues — a step introduced in 2016 to make the process more transparent.

Whoever wins will face major challenges, including internal reforms, severe funding shortfalls, climate change, artificial intelligence, and rising geopolitical tensions. Experts say the job depends heavily on the individual who takes it.
why_it_matters: The person in this job helps shape how the world responds to problems that cross borders — wars, climate change, and now artificial intelligence — so who gets chosen, and who gets left out, affects young people everywhere for years.

background_read: The United Nations (an organization founded in 1945, after World War II, where almost every country meets to discuss global problems) now has 193 member states, and its Charter set up the job of secretary-general from the start.

António Guterres (the UN's secretary-general, in office since 2017) is the ninth person to hold the post — and every one of the nine so far has been a man, which is why the possibility of a first woman leader is drawing so much attention.

The choice is split between two bodies: the General Assembly (where all member states have one vote) formally appoints, while the Security Council (whose five permanent members — the United States, Russia, China, France and Britain — hold veto power) recommends. That means one permanent member can quietly block a candidate.

The idea that the job rotates between regions is only an informal tradition, not a written rule. Latin America and the Caribbean held it decades ago but not since, which is part of why a candidate from that region is seen as likely this time.

perspectives.perspective: Reformers who want a more open UN
perspectives.description: They point out that public town halls and interactive dialogues, introduced in 2016, let the world actually hear from candidates — and see the possibility of a first woman leader as proof the institution can modernize. For them, a more transparent and representative process makes the UN more credible.

They argue the real decision happens behind closed doors in the Security Council, where any one of the five permanent members can veto a candidate. The claim of a 'race' can look like theater when the shortlist and the outcome are largely negotiated by the most powerful states.

Experts like Richard Gowan stress that the secretary-general commands no army and controls no large budget, so influence depends on persuasion, public standing and the individual's skill. The same job can look weak or hugely consequential depending on who holds it.

Whoever takes office in 2027 inherits funding shortfalls, demands for internal reform, climate pressure and rising great-power rivalry. Some suggest that pressure could push member states to formalize the regional rotation and transparency rules — or that big powers will resist and keep the informal system exactly as it is.
